findings: Input size: empirical time growth exponent (log-log slope; 1.0=linear, n log n appears as ~1.05-1.15): merge_sort (w=1): 1.103, parallel_merge_sort (w=1): 1.083, parallel_merge_sort (w=2): 1.088, parallel_merge_sort (w=4): 1.014, parallel_merge_sort (w=8): 1.003, quick_sort (w=1): 1.106, timsort (w=1): 1.17.
Worker count at n=500,000: speedup vs serial merge sort 1w=0.95x (eff 95%), 2w=1.63x (eff 81%), 4w=2.61x (eff 65%), 8w=4.03x (eff 50%).
Saturation (going to more workers gave <1.25x extra gain): n=10,000: 2->4 workers gain 1.179x.
Process-pool startup overhead (measured separately, excluded from exec time): 1w=220.4 ms, 2w=230.8 ms, 4w=278.9 ms, 8w=351.1 ms.

Overheads at n=500,000: IPC/pickling ~5.2% and final k-way merge in the parent ~15.2% of parallel execution time on average across worker counts; the merge is serial and grows with worker count, limiting scalability (Amdahl's law).

Load balance (max/mean worker sort time, 1.00=perfect): 1w=1.000, 2w=1.014, 4w=1.095, 8w=1.082. Chunks differ by at most one element, so imbalance comes from OS scheduling/SMT sharing rather than uneven work.
Serial merge sort beats a one-off parallel sort (including pool startup) at n = 10,000, 25,000, 50,000, 75,000, 100,000.
Parallel merge sort with 1 worker is slower than serial merge sort by 7.5% on average: pure overhead of pickling data to/from a worker process.
Built-in Timsort (C implementation, serial) beats the best pure-Python parallel merge sort at 9/9 input sizes: implementation efficiency outweighs multicore parallelism here.
